claim: Canonical transient receptor channels (TRPC) are non-selective cation channels.
source: Canonical transient receptor channels (TRPC) are non-selective cation channels.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about TRPC channels presented in the abstract.

claim: TRPC channels are involved in receptor-operated Ca2+ signaling.
source: They are involved in receptor-operated Ca2+ signaling and have been proposed to act as store-operated channels (SOC).
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about TRPC function.

claim: TRPC channels have been proposed to act as store-operated channels (SOC).
source: They are involved in receptor-operated Ca2+ signaling and have been proposed to act as store-operated channels (SOC).
evidence: The use of 'have been proposed' indicates this is based on prior research in the field.

claim: Malfunction of TRPC channels is related to cardiomyopathies.
source: Their malfunction is related to cardiomyopathies and their modulation by small molecules has been shown to be effective against renal cancer cells.
evidence: This is stated as an established relationship between TRPC malfunction and disease.

claim: Modulation of TRPC channels by small molecules has been shown to be effective against renal cancer cells.
source: Their malfunction is related to cardiomyopathies and their modulation by small molecules has been shown to be effective against renal cancer cells.
evidence: The phrase 'has been shown' indicates this is based on prior experimental evidence.

claim: The molecular mechanism underlying the complex activation and regulation of TRPC channels is poorly understood.
source: The molecular mechanism underlying the complex activation and regulation is poorly understood.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The electron cryo-microscopy structure of zebrafish TRPC4 in its unliganded (apo), closed state was determined at an overall resolution of 3.6 Å.
source: Here, we report the electron cryo-microscopy structure of zebrafish TRPC4 in its unliganded (apo), closed state at an overall resolution of 3.6 Å.
evidence: This is the primary experimental result reported in the manuscript, supported by the cryo-EM data and analysis described in the methods and results.

claim: The TRPC4 structure reveals the molecular architecture of the cation conducting pore, including the selectivity filter and lower gate.
source: The structure reveals the molecular architecture of the cation conducting pore, including the selectivity filter and lower gate.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data and detailed analysis of the pore region presented in the results section.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of TRPC4 contains two key hubs that have been shown to interact with modulating proteins.
source: The cytoplasmic domain contains two key hubs that have been shown to interact with modulating proteins.
evidence: This combines structural observations from the current study with prior biochemical evidence of protein interactions.

claim: TRP channels constitute a large superfamily of ion channels that can be grouped in seven subfamilies: TRPC, TRPM, TRPML, TRPP, TRPV, TRPA and TRPN.
source: Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels constitute a large superfamily of ion channels that can be grouped in seven subfamilies: TRPC, TRPM, TRPML, TRPP, TRPV, TRPA and TRPN (Montell, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation to Montell, 2005.

claim: The channels of the TRP superfamily are diverse in respect to modes of activities, ion selectivity and physiological functions.
source: The channels of the TRP superfamily are diverse in respect to modes of activities, ion selectivity and physiological functions.
evidence: This is a general characterization of TRP channels based on established knowledge.

claim: Most TRP channels are non-selective cation channels with varying preferences for Ca2+ over Na+.
source: Most TRP channels are non-selective cation channels with varying preferences for Ca2+ over Na+ (Owsianik et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a general statement about TRP channel properties supported by a citation.

claim: Some TRPs are physically stimulated or voltage-activated, whereas others respond to the binding of ligands or the direct interaction with other proteins.
source: Some TRPs are physically stimulated or voltage-activated, whereas others respond to the binding of ligands or the direct interaction with other proteins.
evidence: This describes the diversity of TRP channel activation mechanisms based on established knowledge.

claim: TRPs are involved in many cellular processes, including mechanosensation, thermosensitivity, nociception and store-operated Ca2+ entry.
source: Corresponding to their functional diversity TRPs are involved in many cellular processes, including mechanosensation, thermosensitivity, nociception and store-operated Ca2+ entry (Nilius and Flockerzi, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TRP channel functions, supported by a citation.

claim: TRPC4 is one of seven members of the subfamily of TRPC (canonical TRPs) channels.
source: TRPC4 is one of seven members of the subfamily of TRPC (canonical TRPs) channels (Freichel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a classification statement supported by a citation.

claim: TRPC channels are Ca2+/Na+-permeable cation channels.
source: TRPC channels are Ca2+/Na+-permeable cation channels that are expressed in many cell types and tissues, including brain, placenta, adrenal gland, retina endothelia, testis, and kidney (Freichel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a characterization of TRPC channel properties supported by a citation.

claim: TRPC channels are expressed in many cell types and tissues, including brain, placenta, adrenal gland, retina endothelia, testis, and kidney.
source: TRPC channels are Ca2+/Na+-permeable cation channels that are expressed in many cell types and tissues, including brain, placenta, adrenal gland, retina endothelia, testis, and kidney (Freichel et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the tissue distribution of TRPC channels, supported by a citation.

claim: TRPC channels play an important role in vasorelaxation and neurotransmitter release.
source: The channels play an important role in vasorelaxation and neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is a statement about TRPC channel function based on established knowledge.

claim: TRPC4 contributes to axonal regeneration after nerve injury.
source: TRPC4 contributes to axonal regeneration after nerve injury (Wu et al., 2008) and TRPC channels in general are necessary mediators of pathologic cardiac hypertrophy (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2008.

claim: TRPC channels in general are necessary mediators of pathologic cardiac hypertrophy.
source: TRPC4 contributes to axonal regeneration after nerve injury (Wu et al., 2008) and TRPC channels in general are necessary mediators of pathologic cardiac hypertrophy (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2010.

claim: The activation mechanism of TRPC4 has been controversially discussed.
source: The activation mechanism of TRPC4 has been controversially discussed (Plant and Schaefer, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Dependent on the cellular environment and method of measurement, the reported activation mechanism, permeability and biophysical properties differ for TRPC4 and its close homologue TRPC5.
source: Dependent on the cellular environment and method of measurement, the reported activation mechanism, permeability and biophysical properties differ for TRPC4 and its close homologue TRPC5 (Plant and Schaefer, 2003).
evidence: This describes variability in reported properties, supported by a citation.

claim: Several studies showed that TRPC4 and TRPC5 form receptor-operated, Ca2+-permeable, non-selective cation channels.
source: Several studies showed that TRPC4 and TRPC5 form receptor-operated, Ca2+-permeable, non-selective cation channels (Okada et al., 1998; Schaefer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: TRPC4 and TRPC5 are activated by Ca2+ store-depletion with moderate to high Ca2+ permeabilities.
source: Others found that TRPC4 and TRPC5 are activated by Ca2+ store-depletion with moderate to high Ca2+ permeabilities (Philipp et al., 1996; Warnat et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Philipp et al., 1996 and Warnat et al., 1999.

claim: TRPC4 directly interacts with IP3 receptors.
source: In line with both findings, TRPC4 directly interacts with IP3 receptors, calmodulin (Mery et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2001), STIM1 (Lee et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008), the lipid-binding protein SESTD1 (Miehe et al., 2010) and the G protein Gαi2 (Jeon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mery et al., 2001 and Tang et al., 2001.

claim: TRPC4 directly interacts with calmodulin.
source: In line with both findings, TRPC4 directly interacts with IP3 receptors, calmodulin (Mery et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2001), STIM1 (Lee et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008), the lipid-binding protein SESTD1 (Miehe et al., 2010) and the G protein Gαi2 (Jeon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mery et al., 2001 and Tang et al., 2001.

claim: TRPC4 directly interacts with STIM1.
source: In line with both findings, TRPC4 directly interacts with IP3 receptors, calmodulin (Mery et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2001), STIM1 (Lee et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008), the lipid-binding protein SESTD1 (Miehe et al., 2010) and the G protein Gαi2 (Jeon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2010 and Zeng et al., 2008.

claim: TRPC4 directly interacts with the lipid-binding protein SESTD1.
source: In line with both findings, TRPC4 directly interacts with IP3 receptors, calmodulin (Mery et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2001), STIM1 (Lee et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008), the lipid-binding protein SESTD1 (Miehe et al., 2010) and the G protein Gαi2 (Jeon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Miehe et al., 2010.

claim: TRPC4 directly interacts with the G protein Gαi2.
source: In line with both findings, TRPC4 directly interacts with IP3 receptors, calmodulin (Mery et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2001), STIM1 (Lee et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008), the lipid-binding protein SESTD1 (Miehe et al., 2010) and the G protein Gαi2 (Jeon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jeon et al., 2012.

claim: SESTD1 binds several phospholipid species and is essential for efficient receptor-mediated activation of TRPC5.
source: SESTD1 binds several phospholipid species and is essential for efficient receptor-mediated activation of TRPC5 (Miehe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Miehe et al., 2010.

claim: TRPC channels have been shown to be activated by NO.
source: In addition, TRPC channels have been shown to be activated by NO (Yoshida et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yoshida et al., 2006.

claim: (-)-Englerin A has been shown to be a potent and selective activator of TRPC4 and TRPC5 calcium channels.
source: Recently, (-)-Englerin A has been shown to be a potent and selective activator of TRPC4 and TRPC5 calcium channels (Akbulut et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Akbulut et al., 2015.

claim: (-)-Englerin A selectively kills renal cancer cells by elevated Ca2+ influx.
source: It selectively kills renal cancer cells by elevated Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of (-)-Englerin A based on prior research.

claim: (-)-Englerin A is so far the only known potent activator of TRPC4 and TRPC5.
source: (-)-Englerin A is so far the only known potent activator of TRPC4 and TRPC5.
evidence: This is a statement about the uniqueness of this compound based on current knowledge.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of TRPV1 ushered structural biology of TRP channels in a new era.
source: The cryo-EM structure of TRPV1 (Liao et al., 2013) ushered structural biology of TRP channels in a new era.
evidence: This is a historical statement about the impact of the TRPV1 structure, supported by a citation.

claim: Structure models for 48 TRP channels from six subfamilies have been published.
source: So far structure models for 48 TRP channels from six subfamilies have been published (Madej and Ziegler, 2018).
evidence: This is a count of published structures, supported by a citation.

claim: The TRPCs represent the only subfamily for which no high-resolution structure has been reported so far.
source: The TRPCs represent the only subfamily for which no high-resolution structure has been reported so far limiting our understanding of these important types of cation channels.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of structural knowledge prior to this work.

claim: Human TRPC4 proved not to be stable enough for structural investigations.
source: Initially, we planned to heterologously express human TRPC4 in HEK293 cells and purify it to determine its structure by single particle cryo-EM. However, the protein proved not to be stable enough for structural investigations.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Wild type TRPC4 from zebrafish (TRPC4DR) was found to be the most suitable for structural studies.
source: We therefore screened TRPC4 orthologues from several different species and found wild type TRPC4 from zebrafish (TRPC4DR) to be the most suitable for our studies.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental screening described in the manuscript.

claim: TRPC4DR has very high sequence similarity to human TRPC4 (76% sequence identity).
source: TRPC4DR has very high sequence similarity to human TRPC4 (76% sequence identity, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Like human TRPC4, TRPC4DR can be activated by (-)-Englerin A resulting in similar currents.
source: The measurements demonstrated that, like human TRPC4 (Akbulut et al., 2015), TRPC4DR can be activated by (-)-Englerin A resulting in similar currents (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 1 and comparison to published data on human TRPC4.

claim: Current-voltage curves (IV-curves) of TRPC4DR in the presence of (-)-Englerin A showed a doubly rectifying form.
source: Of note, current-voltage curves (IV-curves) in the presence of (-)-Englerin A showed a doubly rectifying form (Figure 1e) and reversal potentials close to 0 mV (−3.2 ± 1.7 mV, n = 6).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: TRPC4DR shows reversal potentials close to 0 mV (−3.2 ± 1.7 mV, n = 6) in the presence of (-)-Englerin A.
source: Of note, current-voltage curves (IV-curves) in the presence of (-)-Englerin A showed a doubly rectifying form (Figure 1e) and reversal potentials close to 0 mV (−3.2 ± 1.7 mV, n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the voltage-clamp experiments.

claim: The doubly rectifying form of the IV-curve is a characteristic hallmark of active TRPC4.
source: The doubly rectifying form of the IV-curve is a characteristic hallmark of active TRPC4 (Akbulut et al., 2015; Freichel et al., 2014; Schaefer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Under asymmetric ion concentrations, reversal potentials close to 0 mV indicate a poor cation selectivity.
source: Under the experimental conditions, namely asymmetric ion concentrations, reversal potentials close to 0 mV indicate a poor cation selectivity, which is a known property of several TRPC4 variants from different species (Freichel et al., 2014; Schaefer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on established biophysical principles and supported by citations.

claim: Poor cation selectivity is a known property of several TRPC4 variants from different species.
source: Under the experimental conditions, namely asymmetric ion concentrations, reversal potentials close to 0 mV indicate a poor cation selectivity, which is a known property of several TRPC4 variants from different species (Freichel et al., 2014; Schaefer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Upon addition of 50 nM of (-)-Englerin A, the current density at −60 mV increased from −3.1 ± 1.9 pA/pF (n = 6) to −16.7 ± 10.7 pA/pF (n = 6) in HEK293 cells expressing TRPC4DR-EGFP.
source: Upon addition of 50 nM of (-)-Englerin A, the current density at −60 mV increased from −3.1 ± 1.9 pA/pF (n = 6) to −16.7 ± 10.7 pA/pF (n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: In untransfected control cells, the current density in the absence and presence of (-)-Englerin A was virtually the same with values of −2.1 ± 1.2 pA/pF (V = - 60 mV, n = 5) and −1.8 ± 0.9 pA/pF (V = −60 mV, n = 5) respectively.
source: In untransfected control cells, the current density in the absence and presence of the activator was virtually the same with values of −2.1 ± 1.2 pA/pF (V = - 60 mV, n = 5) and −1.8 ± 0.9 pA/pF (V = −60 mV, n = 5) respectively.
evidence: This is a control experiment result shown in Figure 1.

claim: The overall structure of the homotetrameric TRPC4DR is similar to that of other TRP channels.
source: The overall structure of the homotetrameric TRPC4DR is similar to that of other TRP channels (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is a structural comparison based on the cryo-EM structure determined in this study.

claim: The transmembrane domain comprising the voltage-sensor-like (VSL) domain and pore domain is structurally conserved in TRPC4DR compared to other TRP channels.
source: Especially the transmembrane domain comprising the voltage-sensor-like (VSL) domain and pore domain is structurally conserved.
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the TRPC4DR structure to other TRP structures.

claim: Like TRPVs, TRPMs, TRPAs and TRPNs, TRPC4DR does not have extracellular but extended cytoplasmic domains.
source: Like TRPVs, TRPMs, TRPAs and TRPNs, TRPC4DR does not have extracellular but extended cytoplasmic domains.
evidence: This is a structural comparison based on the TRPC4DR structure and known structures of other TRP channels.

claim: The resolved regions of the cytoplasmic domain of TRPC4DR reaches ~80 Å into the cytosol.
source: The resolved regions of the cytoplasmic domain of TRPC4DR reaches ~80 Å into the cytosol and is relatively short compared to other TRP channels.
evidence: This is a measurement from the TRPC4DR structure.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of TRPC4DR is relatively short compared to other TRP channels.
source: The resolved regions of the cytoplasmic domain of TRPC4DR reaches ~80 Å into the cytosol and is relatively short compared to other TRP channels.
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation.

claim: The upper part of the cytoplasmic domain comprises a conserved TRP domain, a pre-S1 elbow domain that enters partially the membrane and an extended helical linker domain.
source: The upper part comprises a conserved TRP domain, a pre-S1 elbow domain that enters partially the membrane and an extended helical linker domain (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the TRPC4DR structure.

claim: The lower part of the cytoplasmic domain is formed by the Rib (or Stretcher) helix, the C-terminal helix and four ankyrin repeats.
source: The lower part is formed by the Rib (or Stretcher) helix, the C-terminal helix and four ankyrin repeats (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This is a description of the structural features observed in the TRPC4DR structure.

claim: 3-D classification and refinement revealed that the lower cytoplasmic part of TRPC4DR is flexible, whereas the transmembrane domain is not.
source: 3-D classification and refinement of the final data set (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) revealed that the lower cytoplasmic part of TRPC4DR is flexible, whereas the transmembrane domain is not (Video 2).
evidence: This is a result from the cryo-EM data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Video 2.

claim: Only some members of the TRP family, such as TRPM8, TRPM4, and TRPP1 have been shown to exhibit mild voltage sensitivity.
source: Although TRP channels contain a structurally conserved VSL domain comprising four helices (S1-S4), only some members of the TRP family, such as TRPM8, TRPM4, and TRPP1 have been shown to exhibit mild voltage sensitivity (Nilius et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2016a; Voets et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Helix S4 harbors the key residues involved in voltage sensing in voltage-gated ion channels.
source: Helix S4 harbors the key residues involved in voltage sensing in voltage-gated ion channels (Swartz, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about voltage-gated ion channels, supported by a citation.

claim: A general motif in the voltage-sensing domain (VSD) of voltage-gated ion channels comprises two sets of basic residues on helix S4 that are stabilized by counteracting acidic residues and separated by a hydrophobic patch.
source: A general motif in the voltage-sensing domain (VSD) of voltage-gated ion channels comprises two sets of basic residues on helix S4 that are stabilized by counteracting acidic residues and separated by a hydrophobic patch (Kim and Nimigean, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about voltage-sensing domains, supported by a citation.

claim: Upon voltage change, helix S4 moves and the positively charged residues jump from one counteracting set of residues over the hydrophobic patch to the next set of negatively charged residues.
source: Upon voltage change, helix S4 moves and the positively charged residues jump from one counteracting set of residues over the hydrophobic patch to the next set of negatively charged residues (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of voltage sensing, supported by a citation.

claim: R491 in TRPC4DR is located at the same position as K302 in the Kv1.2-Kv2.1 paddle chimera, corresponding to the lower pair of electrostatically interacting residues.
source: Comparing the VSL domain in our structure and other TRP channels with the VSD in the structure of the Kv1.2-Kv2.1 paddle chimera (Long et al., 2007), we found that R491 in TRPC4DR is located at the same position as K302 in the potassium channel, corresponding to the lower pair of electrostatically interacting residues (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a structural comparison based on the TRPC4DR structure and the Kv1.2-Kv2.1 structure.

claim: At the position equivalent to R491 in TRPC4DR, an arginine has been observed in TRPM4 and TRPM8, and a lysine in TRPP1.
source: At this position an arginine has been observed in TRPM4 and TRPM8 (Winkler et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2018), and a lysine in TRPP1 (Shen et al., 2016b) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a structural comparison based on published structures of other TRP channels.

claim: In all TRP channels examined, the basic residues at the position equivalent to R491 in TRPC4DR are stabilized by interaction with acidic residues.
source: In all cases, the basic residues are stabilized by interaction with acidic residues.
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparisons shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There are no equivalently interacting residues in TRPV1 at the position corresponding to R491 in TRPC4DR.
source: Importantly, there are no equivalently interacting residues in TRPV1 at this position (Liao et al., 2013) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a structural comparison based on the TRPV1 structure.

claim: The hydrophobic patch is more prominent in all compared TRP channels than in the Kv1.2-Kv2.1 paddle chimera.
source: The hydrophobic patch that has been shown to maintain the electric field across the membrane by preventing the movement of ions (Lacroix et al., 2014) is more prominent in all compared TRP channels than in the Kv1.2-Kv2.1 paddle chimera (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The second pair of interacting basic and acidic residues essential for S4 movement in Kv1.2 cannot be found in the TRP channels.
source: However, the second pair of interacting basic and acidic residues, which is essential for the movement of helix S4 comprising residues R290, R293, E183 and E226 in Kv1.2, cannot be found in the TRP channels.
evidence: This is a structural comparison between TRP channels and voltage-gated potassium channels.

claim: TRPM8 has two residues with complementary charges at the position of the second pair of interacting residues in Kv1.2, however, these residues point away from each other in the structure and do not interact.
source: Only TRPM8 has two residues with complementary charges at this position, however, these residues point away from each other in the structure and do not interact (Yin et al., 2018) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the TRPM8 structure.

claim: The mechanism of voltage gating in TRP channels must differ from that of voltage-gated ion channels.
source: Thus, the mechanism of voltage gating in TRP channels must differ from that of voltage-gated ion channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural comparisons showing differences in key residues.

claim: Positively charged residues involved in voltage sensing in Kv1.2 (R293, R296, R299, R302, R305, and K308) are replaced by polar residues (N485, S488, S494, and T497) in TRPC4DR.
source: Interestingly, positively charged residues that are involved in voltage sensing in Kv1.2, such as R293, R296, R299, R302, R305, and K308 are replaced by polar residues, including N485, S488, S494, and T497 in TRPC4DR.
evidence: This is a structural comparison between TRPC4DR and Kv1.2.

claim: The VSL domain in other TRP channels contains more hydrophobic residues than TRPC4DR.
source: The VSL domain in other TRP channels contains more hydrophobic residues (Liao et al., 2013; Winkler et al., 2017) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 3b and supported by citations.

claim: The pre-S1 elbow domain sits inside the membrane and forms a cavity with helices S1 and S4 in which a sterol was identified.
source: Upstream of the VSL domain resides the pre-S1 elbow domain. It sits inside the membrane and forms a cavity with helices S1 and S4 in which we could identify density corresponding to a sterol (Figure 4a–b).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the TRPC4DR cryo-EM map.

claim: A CHS molecule was fitted into the density in the cavity formed by the pre-S1 elbow domain and helices S1 and S4.
source: Since we added CHS during the purification of TRPC4DR, we fitted this molecule into the density.
evidence: This is based on the experimental conditions and the observed density in the structure.

claim: A CHS molecule has been found at the same position in the structures of TRPM4 and TRPML3.
source: Interestingly, a CHS molecule has also been found at the same position in the structures of TRPM4 (Autzen et al., 2018) and TRPML3 (Hirschi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to other published TRP channel structures.

claim: In a cavity between the pre-S1 elbow domain and helices S1 and S2 resides a proline-rich repeat connecting the TRP and helical linker domains.
source: In a second cavity between the pre-S1 elbow domain and helices S1 and S2 resides a proline-rich repeat connecting the TRP and helical linker domains (see below).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the TRPC4DR structure.

claim: The four coordinating residues for Ca2+ binding in Ca2+-activated TRPM4 are conserved in TRPC4.
source: Interestingly, the four coordinating residues that have been reported for binding of Ca2+ in Ca2+-activated TRPM4 (Autzen et al., 2018) are conserved in TRPC4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation and structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the TRPC4DR structure, the position of the conserved Ca2+-coordinating residues is very similar to TRPM4 and would allow the coordination of a Ca2+ ion.
source: In the TRPC4DR structure, their position is very similar to TRPM4 and would allow the coordination of a Ca2+ ion (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: An extra density was observed at the center between the conserved Ca2+-coordinating residues in TRPC4DR, but it was not assigned to Ca2+ because of the limited resolution.
source: Although we indeed observed an extra density at the center between these residues, we did not assign it to Ca2+ because of the limited resolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM map with a cautious interpretation due to resolution limitations.

claim: Like in other TRP channels, helix S5 and S6 swap over to the respective helices of the adjacent protomer and form the pore at the center of the tetrameric channel.
source: Like in other TRP channels, helix S5 and S6 swap over to the respective helices of the adjacent protomer and form the pore at the center of the tetrameric channel (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a structural observation consistent with other TRP channel structures.

claim: The extracellular opening of the pore in TRPC4DR is negatively charged.
source: The extracellular opening of the pore is negatively charged (Figure 5a) and the residue E555 at the tip of the pore turret, which is conserved in TRPC1, TRPC4, and TRPC5 (Liu et al., 2003), forms a salt bridge with R556 of the adjacent protomer (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b).
evidence: This is shown in the electrostatic surface representation in Figure 5a.

claim: The residue E555 at the tip of the pore turret is conserved in TRPC1, TRPC4, and TRPC5.
source: The extracellular opening of the pore is negatively charged (Figure 5a) and the residue E555 at the tip of the pore turret, which is conserved in TRPC1, TRPC4, and TRPC5 (Liu et al., 2003), forms a salt bridge with R556 of the adjacent protomer (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b).
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation and supported by a citation.

claim: E555 forms a salt bridge with R556 of the adjacent protomer in TRPC4DR.
source: The extracellular opening of the pore is negatively charged (Figure 5a) and the residue E555 at the tip of the pore turret, which is conserved in TRPC1, TRPC4, and TRPC5 (Liu et al., 2003), forms a salt bridge with R556 of the adjacent protomer (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b.

claim: The salt bridge between E555 and R556 results in a positioning of E555 away from the pore and in a relatively wide opening of its entrance similar to TRPV1.
source: This results in a positioning of E555 away from the pore and in a relatively wide opening of its entrance similar to TRPV1 (Liao et al., 2013) (Figure 5b–d).
evidence: This is a structural observation and comparison to TRPV1 shown in Figure 5b–d.

claim: The wide pore opening in TRPC4DR is in contrast to the narrow pore openings of the more selective Ca2+ channels TRPV5 and TRPV6.
source: This is in contrast to the narrow pore openings of the more selective Ca2+ channels TRPV5 (Hughes et al., 2018) and TRPV6 (McGoldrick et al., 2018) and possibly explains the lower selectivity of TRPC4 channels.
evidence: This is a structural comparison to other TRP channels with different selectivity properties.

claim: The wide pore opening possibly explains the lower selectivity of TRPC4 channels.
source: This is in contrast to the narrow pore openings of the more selective Ca2+ channels TRPV5 (Hughes et al., 2018) and TRPV6 (McGoldrick et al., 2018) and possibly explains the lower selectivity of TRPC4 channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison and known selectivity properties.

claim: Mutation of E555 (E559 in TRPC1) to lysine results in decreased store-operated Ca2+ influx.
source: Mutation of E555 (E559 in TRPC1) to lysine results in decreased store-operated Ca2+ influx (Liu et al., 2003), suggesting that a negatively charged and stable pore opening is crucial for the undisturbed permeation of cations through TRPCs.
evidence: This is based on published mutagenesis data.

claim: A negatively charged and stable pore opening is crucial for the undisturbed permeation of cations through TRPCs.
source: Mutation of E555 (E559 in TRPC1) to lysine results in decreased store-operated Ca2+ influx (Liu et al., 2003), suggesting that a negatively charged and stable pore opening is crucial for the undisturbed permeation of cations through TRPCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutagenesis data and structural observations.

claim: The selectivity filter in TRPC4DR is formed by four glycine residues (G577) that constrict the pore to a diameter of 7.0 Å (3.7 Å defined by opposing van der Waals surfaces).
source: The selectivity filter is formed by four glycine residues (G577) that constrict the pore to a diameter of 7.0 Å (3.7 Å defined by opposing van der Waals surfaces) (Figure 5c–d).
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the TRPC4DR structure shown in Figure 5c–d.

claim: Cations are likely partly dehydrated when passing through the selectivity filter of TRPC4DR.
source: Since the diameters of Na+ and Ca2+ ions are ~2 Å in their dehydrated and ~10–12 Å in their fully hydrated state, the cations are likely partly dehydrated when passing through the selectivity filter.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured pore diameter and known ion sizes.

claim: Neither the diameter of the selectivity filter nor the type of residue correlates with the selectivity of TRP channels for Na+ or Ca2+.
source: Although TRPs differ in their cation selectivity, there is no clear factor recognizable that determines the level of selectivity (Table 2). Neither the diameter of the filter, ranging from 1.8 to 8.4 Å, nor the type of residue, mostly glycine or aspartate, correlates with the selectivity of the channels for Na+ or Ca2+ (Table 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparative analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The level of selectivity in TRP channels must be defined differently than by the diameter or residue type of the selectivity filter.
source: The level of selectivity must therefore be defined differently.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of correlation between structural features and selectivity.

claim: S580 resides directly above the selectivity filter in TRPC4DR.
source: Directly above the selectivity filter resides S580 (Figure 5c–d) which is replaced by an asparagine residue in human TRPC4 and TRPC5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 5c–d.

claim: S580 in zebrafish TRPC4 is replaced by an asparagine residue in human TRPC4 and TRPC5.
source: Directly above the selectivity filter resides S580 (Figure 5c–d) which is replaced by an asparagine residue in human TRPC4 and TRPC5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The residue at position 580 in TRPC5 has been shown to be important for Ca2+ permeability.
source: In TRPC5 this residue has been shown to be important for Ca2+ permeability (Chen et al., 2017b) and in TRPV1 D646, located at a similar position, has been identified as important residue for cation selection (García-Martínez et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on published mutagenesis studies.

claim: In TRPV1, D646, located at a similar position to S580 in TRPC4DR, has been identified as important residue for cation selection.
source: In TRPC5 this residue has been shown to be important for Ca2+ permeability (Chen et al., 2017b) and in TRPV1 D646, located at a similar position, has been identified as important residue for cation selection (García-Martínez et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on published mutagenesis studies.

claim: The lumen of the pore below the selectivity filter is mainly hydrophobic.
source: The lumen of the pore below the selectivity filter is mainly hydrophobic (Figure 5b) and leads to the lower gate at the cytoplasmic end formed by the conserved residues I617 and N621 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is shown in the hydrophobicity analysis in Figure 5b.

claim: The lower gate at the cytoplasmic end of the pore is formed by the conserved residues I617 and N621.
source: The lumen of the pore below the selectivity filter is mainly hydrophobic (Figure 5b) and leads to the lower gate at the cytoplasmic end formed by the conserved residues I617 and N621 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 5c.

claim: I617 belongs to the M3 motif found in all TRPCs, TRPVs, and TRPMs.
source: I617 belongs to the M3 motif found in all TRPCs, TRPVs, and TRPMs (Freichel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation and supported by a citation.

claim: The TRPC4DR channel is almost completely closed in the structure.
source: In our case, the TRPC4DR channel is almost completely closed.
evidence: This is a description of the conformational state observed in the structure.

claim: The four isoleucines and four asparagines at the lower gate constrict the pore to a diameter of ~5.3 and ~4.2 Å, respectively (1.6 and 0.7 Å defined by opposing van der Waals surfaces).
source: The four isoleucines and four asparagines constrict the pore to a diameter of ~5.3 and ~4.2 Å, respectively (1.6 and 0.7 Å defined by opposing van der Waals surfaces) (Figure 5c–d).
evidence: This is a structural measurement shown in Figure 5c–d.

claim: Ca2+ and Na+ ions are too large to fit through the constrictions at the lower gate even in a dehydrated state.
source: Ca2+ and Na+ ions are too large to fit through these constrictions even in a dehydrated state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured pore diameter and known ion sizes.

claim: The lower constriction of the TRPP channel PKD2 is also formed by an asparagine and leads to a closure of the pore.
source: The lower constriction of the TRPP channel PKD2 is also formed by an asparagine and leads to a closure of the pore (Shen et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a comparison to another TRP channel structure, supported by a citation.

claim: Below the asparagine and very close to the cytoplasmic end of the pore, a glutamine (Q625) points towards the pore.
source: Below the asparagine and very close to the cytoplasmic end of the pore, a glutamine (Q625) points towards the pore (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Q625 is conserved in all TRPCs.
source: This residue is conserved in all TRPCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), however, its significance has remained unknown.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The LFW motif (residues 571–573) is conserved in TRPC1 and TRPC5.
source: An important region inside the pore domain is the LFW motif (residues 571–573), which is also conserved in TRPC1 and TRPC5.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation.

claim: Mutation of the LFW motif to AAA in TRPC5 results in non-functional but folded channels.
source: In TRPC5, mutation of the LFW motif to AAA results in non-functional but folded channels (Strübing et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on published mutagenesis data.

claim: In the TRPC4DR structure, F572 and W573 form part of a prominent hydrophobic contact between the pore helix of one protomer and helix S6 of the adjacent protomer, stabilizing the pore.
source: In our TrpC4DR structure F572 and W573 form part of a prominent hydrophobic contact between the pore helix of one protomer and helix S6 of the adjacent protomer, stabilizing the pore (Figure 2—figure supplement 5c–d).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5c–d.

claim: The triple AAA mutation in the LFW motif region likely destabilizes the hydrophobic interaction and results in the collapse of the pore explaining the inactivity of the channel.
source: The triple AAA mutation in this region likely destabilizes this interaction and results in the collapse of the pore explaining the inactivity of the channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation and the mutagenesis data.

claim: An additional density corresponding to an annular lipid was found at the interface near the LFW motif.
source: Interestingly, we found an additional density corresponding to an annular lipid at this interface (Figure 4a,c).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 4a,c.

claim: The shape of the lipid density clearly corresponds to phosphatidic acid (PA) or ceramide-1 phosphate.
source: The shape of the density clearly corresponds to phosphatidic acid (PA) or ceramide-1 phosphate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the density shape.

claim: PA was fitted into the lipid density because PA has been assigned to a similar density found in polycytin-2 and PA has been included in the purification buffer.
source: Since PA has been assigned to a similar density found in polycytin-2 (Wilkes et al., 2017) and PA has been included in our purification buffer we fitted PA into the density (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on comparison to another structure and the experimental conditions.

claim: The phosphate head group of PA interacts with the peptide backbone nitrogen and the polar side chains of T599 of helix S6 and the side chain amino and amide groups of W573 and Q569 of the pore helix.
source: The phosphate head group interacts with the peptide backbone nitrogen and the polar side chains of T599 of helix S6 and the side chain amino and amide groups of W573 and Q569 of the pore helix, respectively (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a structural observation of the lipid-protein interactions shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The non-polar tail group of PA is stabilized by interaction with multiple hydrophobic residues from the surrounding helices S5, S6 and the pore helix.
source: The non-polar tail group is stabilized by interaction with multiple hydrophobic residues from the surrounding helices S5, S6 and the pore helix (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The pore domain contains two cysteines (C549 and C554) that have been studied in relation to S-nitrosylation.
source: Another well-studied region of the pore domain contains two cysteines (C549 and C554). Yoshida et al. showed that S-nitrosylation of these residues in TRPC5 leads to the activation of the channel (Yoshida et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on published biochemical studies.

claim: S-nitrosylation of C549 and C554 in TRPC5 leads to the activation of the channel.
source: Another well-studied region of the pore domain contains two cysteines (C549 and C554). Yoshida et al. showed that S-nitrosylation of these residues in TRPC5 leads to the activation of the channel (Yoshida et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on published biochemical studies.

claim: Yoshida et al. proposed that the modification of C549 and C554 has a direct effect on the conformation of helix S6, resulting in the opening of the gate.
source: The authors proposed that the modification of the residues has a direct effect on the conformation of helix S6, resulting in the opening of the gate.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the cited study.

claim: In the TRPC4 structure, C549 and C554 do not locate in close proximity to helix S6.
source: In the TRPC4 structure, however, C549 and C554 do not locate in close proximity to helix S6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b.

claim: A direct interaction between C549/C554 and helix S6 can be excluded based on the TRPC4 structure.
source: We can therefore exclude a direct interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural observation.

claim: C549 and C554 form a disulfide bridge in TRPC4DR.
source: The cysteines form a disulfide bridge in TRPC4DR (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b) and are likely involved in putting E555 in place, which is located at the extracellular vestibule above the selectivity filter (see above).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b.

claim: C549 and C554 are likely involved in putting E555 in place at the extracellular vestibule above the selectivity filter.
source: The cysteines form a disulfide bridge in TRPC4DR (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a–b) and are likely involved in putting E555 in place, which is located at the extracellular vestibule above the selectivity filter (see above).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural proximity and connectivity.

claim: Nitrosylation reduces the disulphide bond of cystines.
source: Nitrosylation, that reduces the disulphide bond of cystines (Yoshida et al., 2006) could thus lead to a destabilization of the upper region of the selectivity filter.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Nitrosylation could lead to a destabilization of the upper region of the selectivity filter in TRPC4.
source: Nitrosylation, that reduces the disulphide bond of cystines (Yoshida et al., 2006) could thus lead to a destabilization of the upper region of the selectivity filter.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observations and known chemistry.

claim: Upon nitrosylation, E555 could be released and orient towards the center of the pore, altering its properties.
source: In this process, E555 could be released and orient towards the center of the pore, altering its properties.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on the structural analysis.

claim: The conformational change resulting from nitrosylation could result in a negatively charged sink at the turret, thereby attracting cations, possibly explaining the effect of the increased Ca2+ conductance.
source: Thus, the conformational change could result in a negatively charged sink at the turret, thereby attracting cations, possibly explaining the effect of the increased Ca2+ conductance observed by Yoshida et al. (Yoshida et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain published observations.

claim: The TRP domain and linker domain connect the transmembrane domain with the lower cytoplasmic domain.
source: The TRP domain and linker domain connect the transmembrane domain with the lower cytoplasmic domain (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 2c–d.

claim: The TRP domain (residues E634 – N658) resides directly after helix S6 and is sandwiched between the linker and transmembrane domains.
source: The TRP domain (residues E634 – N658) resides directly after helix S6 and is sandwiched between the linker and transmembrane domains.
evidence: This is a structural description of the TRP domain location.

claim: The TRP domain is conserved in all TRP subfamilies except TRPPs and TRPMLs.
source: It is conserved in all TRP subfamilies except TRPPs and TRPMLs (Madej and Ziegler, 2018; Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TRP domain conservation, supported by citations.

claim: The core of the TRP domain consists of the conserved WKXQR TRP box sequence (residues 635–639).
source: The core of the TRP domain consists of the conserved WKXQR TRP box sequence (residues 635–639).
evidence: This is a structural and sequence observation.

claim: The central residue W635 of the TRP box has been shown to be of crucial importance for gating of several TRP channels.
source: Its central residue W635 has been shown to be of crucial importance for gating of several TRP channels.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on prior studies.

claim: Mutation of W635 in TRPV3 leads to Olmsted syndrome.
source: Its mutation in TRPV3 leads to Olmsted syndrome (Lin et al., 2012) and in NOMPC an exchange to alanine results in a channel with a prominent basal current that does not respond to mechanical stimuli anymore (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on published genetic and functional studies.

claim: In NOMPC, exchange of W635 to alanine results in a channel with a prominent basal current that does not respond to mechanical stimuli anymore.
source: Its mutation in TRPV3 leads to Olmsted syndrome (Lin et al., 2012) and in NOMPC an exchange to alanine results in a channel with a prominent basal current that does not respond to mechanical stimuli anymore (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on published mutagenesis and functional studies.

claim: Like in other TRP domain-containing TRPs, W635 in TRPC4DR interacts with the conserved G503 in the adjacent M2 motif thereby linking the TRP domain with the linker between helices S4-S5.
source: Like in other TRP domain-containing TRPs, W635 in TRPC4DR interacts with the conserved G503 in the adjacent M2 motif (residues 502–511) thereby linking the TRP domain with the linker between helices S4-S5 (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 6a–b and consistent with other TRP structures.

claim: G503 is conserved in all TRP subfamilies containing a TRP domain.
source: G503 is conserved in all TRP subfamilies containing a TRP domain (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Mutation of G503 to serine in TRPC4 and TRPC5 forces the channels in an open conformation.
source: Mutation of this residue to serine in TRPC4 and TRPC5 forces the channels in an open conformation (Beck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on published mutagenesis studies.

claim: The proper interaction between G503 and W635 guarantees the stabilization of helix S6 that forms the lower gate of the pore.
source: The proper interaction between G503 and W635 guarantees the stabilization of helix S6 that forms the lower gate of the pore.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and mutagenesis data.

claim: A G503S or W635A mutation would impair the interaction between G503 and W635 and result in the loss of control over the gate.
source: It becomes clear from looking at these residues in our TRPC4DR structure, that a G503S or W635A mutation would impair the interaction at this site and result in the loss of control over the gate (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: E648 and E649 are conserved in TRPC4 and TRPC5.
source: E648 and E649 which are conserved in TRPC4 and TRPC5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) are located at a peripheral loop of the TRP domain (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: E648 and E649 are located at a peripheral loop of the TRP domain.
source: E648 and E649 which are conserved in TRPC4 and TRPC5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) are located at a peripheral loop of the TRP domain (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The glutamates E648 and E649 interact electrostatically with two lysine residues (K684 and K685) in Stim1 proteins resulting in the activation of cation currents.
source: The glutamates interact electrostatically with two lysine residues (K684 and K685) in Stim1 proteins resulting in the activation of cation currents (Lee et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on published biochemical studies.

claim: E648 and E649 are exposed at the periphery of TRPC4DR and are accessible for interactions with other proteins.
source: In line with this biochemical finding, E648 and E649 (E649 is not resolved in our structure) are exposed at the periphery of TRPC4DR (Figure 7a) and are accessible for interactions with other proteins.
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 7a that is consistent with biochemical data.

claim: TRPC4DR contains two conserved proline-rich regions downstream of the TRP domain.
source: TRPC4DR contains two conserved proline-rich regions downstream of the TRP domain.
evidence: This is a sequence and structural observation.

claim: The first proline-rich region formed by P654, P655, P656 re-enters the membrane and is sandwiched between the pre-S1 elbow domain and helix S2 making it inaccessible from the cytoplasm or the membrane.
source: In TRPC4DR the first proline-rich region formed by P654, P655, P656 re-enters the membrane and is sandwiched between the pre-S1 elbow domain and helix S2 making it inaccessible from the cytoplasm or the membrane.
evidence: This is a structural observation about the location and accessibility of this region.

claim: The second proline-rich region around the residues P661 and P663 is not resolved in the TRPC4DR structure but this region is located at the outside of the protein and could thereby be accessible for interacting with regulatory proteins like Homer.
source: The second proline-rich region around the residues P661 and P663 is not resolved in our structure but this region is located at the outside of the protein and could thereby be accessible for interacting with regulatory proteins like Homer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural context and known protein interactions.

claim: Homer is an adaptor protein that facilitates the physical interaction between TRPC1 and the IP3 receptor.
source: Homer is an adaptor protein that facilitates the physical interaction between TRPC1 and the IP3 receptor (Yuan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The helical linker domain is made of three layers of helices that are arranged like stair steps and a coil of shorter helices.
source: The helical linker domain is made of three layers of helices that are arranged like stair steps and a coil of shorter helices (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a structural description shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The upper layer of helices in the helical linker domain harbors the M1 motif (residues 285–319), which is conserved in the TRPC family.
source: The upper layer of helices harbors the M1 motif (residues 285–319), which is conserved in the TRPC family (Flockerzi, 2007).
evidence: This is a structural and sequence observation supported by a citation.

claim: The central two helices of the helical linker domain form a short coiled-coil structure that harbors the multimerization motif (residues D254 -Q302).
source: The central two helices form a short coiled-coil structure that harbors the multimerization motif (residues D254 -Q302), that has been predicted to be involved in the multimerization of TRPCs (Freichel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a structural observation consistent with prior predictions.

claim: The multimerization motif has been predicted to be involved in the multimerization of TRPCs.
source: The central two helices form a short coiled-coil structure that harbors the multimerization motif (residues D254 -Q302), that has been predicted to be involved in the multimerization of TRPCs (Freichel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a prior prediction supported by a citation.

claim: In contrast to other TRP family members, the helical linker domain in TRPC4DR not only connects the transmembrane domain with the lower cytoplasmic domain but also strongly interacts with the adjacent linker domains thereby stabilizing the tetramer.
source: Indeed, in contrast to other TRP family members (Madej and Ziegler, 2018), the helical linker domain does not only connect the transmembrane domain with the lower cytoplasmic domain but also strongly interacts with the adjacent linker domains thereby stabilizing the tetramer (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is a structural observation that distinguishes TRPC4DR from other TRP channels.

claim: This kind of inter-protomer interaction via the helical linker domain has not been observed in the structures of other TRP subfamily members, such as TRPA1, NOMPC and TRPM4.
source: This kind of interaction has not been observed in the structures of other TRP subfamily members, such as TRPA1 (Paulsen et al., 2015), NOMPC (Jin et al., 2017) and TRPM4 (Autzen et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2017a; Winkler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation supported by citations to other TRP structures.

claim: In the TRPV subfamily, the cytoplasmic inter-protomer interaction is mediated between the ankyrin repeat domain of one protomer and the β-strand linker domain of the adjacent protomer.
source: In the TRPV subfamily, the cytoplasmic inter-protomer interaction is mediated between the ankyrin repeat domain of one protomer and the β-strand linker domain of the adjacent protomer (Liao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to the TRPV subfamily structure, supported by a citation.

claim: Ankyrin repeats, the Rib helix, and C-terminal helix domain constitute the most distant region of TRPC4DR.
source: Ankyrin repeats, the Rib helix, and C-terminal helix domain constitute the most distant region of TRPC4DR (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This is a structural description shown in Figure 2c–d.

claim: Ankyrin repeats are often involved in protein-protein interactions.
source: Ankyrin repeats, that are often involved in protein-protein interactions (Sedgwick and Smerdon, 1999), are abundant in TRP channels in varying numbers, ranging from 0 in TRPP (Shen et al., 2016b) and TRPML (Chen et al., 2017a; Hirschi et al., 2017; Schmiege et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2017) to 29 in NOMPC (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ankyrin repeats supported by citations.

claim: Ankyrin repeats are abundant in TRP channels in varying numbers, ranging from 0 in TRPP and TRPML to 29 in NOMPC.
source: Ankyrin repeats, that are often involved in protein-protein interactions (Sedgwick and Smerdon, 1999), are abundant in TRP channels in varying numbers, ranging from 0 in TRPP (Shen et al., 2016b) and TRPML (Chen et al., 2017a; Hirschi et al., 2017; Schmiege et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2017) to 29 in NOMPC (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of ankyrin repeat numbers across TRP subfamilies, supported by citations.

claim: In most structures of TRPs the first ankyrin repeats are oriented in a parallel fashion like in TRPA1.
source: In most structures of TRPs the first ankyrin repeats are oriented in a parallel fashion like in TRPA1 (Paulsen et al., 2015) (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 8a and supported by a citation.

claim: TRPCs contain four ankyrin repeats in the cytoplasmic domain.
source: TRPCs contain four ankyrin repeats in the cytoplasmic domain.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: Biochemical studies have shown that at least the first ankyrin repeat is necessary in TRPC5 for proper tetramerization and function of the channel.
source: Biochemical studies have shown that at least the first ankyrin repeat is necessary in TRPC5 for proper tetramerization and function of the channel (Schindl et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on published biochemical studies.

claim: In the structure of TRPC4DR the ankyrin repeats take a unique twisted orientation and swap over to an adjacent protomer interacting with the C-terminal helix domain and Rib domain explaining the ankyrin repeat's stabilizing effect on the tetramer.
source: In the structure of TRPC4DR the repeats take a unique twisted orientation and swap over to an adjacent protomer interacting with the C-terminal helix domain and Rib domain explaining the ankyrin repeat's stabilizing effect on the tetramer (Figures 2b and 8b).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figures 2b and 8b that explains prior biochemical findings.

claim: The Rib helix runs almost parallel to the membrane and protrudes from the cytoplasmic domain.
source: The Rib helix runs almost parallel to the membrane and protrudes from the cytoplasmic domain (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The Rib helix contains a dual calmodulin- and IP3 receptor-binding site (CIRB).
source: It contains a dual calmodulin- and IP3 receptor-binding site (CIRB) (Mery et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2001) and has been described as binding hub not only for these proteins but also for SESTD1 (Miehe et al., 2010) and the G protein Gαi2 (Jeon et al., 2012) (Zhu, 2005).
evidence: This is based on published biochemical studies.

claim: The Rib helix has been described as binding hub for calmodulin, IP3 receptor, SESTD1, and the G protein Gαi2.
source: It contains a dual calmodulin- and IP3 receptor-binding site (CIRB) (Mery et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2001) and has been described as binding hub not only for these proteins but also for SESTD1 (Miehe et al., 2010) and the G protein Gαi2 (Jeon et al., 2012) (Zhu, 2005).
evidence: This is based on published biochemical studies.

claim: The Rib helix is a central interaction site for TRPC4-modulating proteins and the activity of the channel might be modulated by a displacement mechanism in which the different modulators compete for the same binding site.
source: It is therefore a central interaction site for TRPC4-modulating proteins and the activity of the channel might be modulated by a displacement mechanism in which the different modulators compete for the same binding site (Zhu, 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism of modulation, supported by a citation.

claim: A homologous helix to the Rib helix has been observed in the structure of TRPM4.
source: A homologous helix has been observed in the structure of TRPM4 (Autzen et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2017a; Winkler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a structural comparison supported by citations.

claim: In the structure of TRPM4 the Rib helix is buried by other domains and only the very tip is accessible from the surface.
source: However, in the structure of TRPM4 the Rib helix is buried by other domains and only the very tip is accessible from the surface (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The Rib helix of TRPC4DR is accessible from the cytoplasm and direct binding of calmodulin or IP3-receptor is possible.
source: The Rib helix of TRPC4DR, however, is accessible from the cytoplasm and direct binding of calmodulin or IP3-receptor is possible (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C-terminal helix domain is a second major protein interaction hub.
source: A second major protein interaction hub is the C-terminal helix domain.
evidence: This is stated based on known protein interactions.

claim: The C-terminal helix domain has only been observed before in TRPA1, TRPM4, and TRPM8.
source: It has only been observed before in TRPA1 (Paulsen et al., 2015), TRPM4 (Autzen et al., 2018) (Guo et al., 2017b; Winkler et al., 2017), and TRPM8 (Yin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to other TRP structures, supported by citations.

claim: In TRPA1, TRPM4, and TRPM8, the C-terminal helix domain has a coiled-coil structure.
source: In all described structures, it has a coiled-coil structure (Figure 9a–b).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 9a–b.

claim: In TRPC4DR, the helices of the C-terminal helix domain run in a parallel fashion.
source: In the case of TRPC4DR, however, the helices run in a parallel fashion (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 9c that distinguishes TRPC4DR from other TRP channels.

claim: The C-terminal helix domain has been shown to bind to the D2 dopamine receptor.
source: The C-terminal helix domain has been shown to bind to the D2 dopamine receptor (Hannan et al., 2008) and spectrin αII and βV which are involved in surface expression and activation of TRPC4 (Odell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on published biochemical studies.

claim: The C-terminal helix domain has been shown to bind to spectrin αII and βV which are involved in surface expression and activation of TRPC4.
source: The C-terminal helix domain has been shown to bind to the D2 dopamine receptor (Hannan et al., 2008) and spectrin αII and βV which are involved in surface expression and activation of TRPC4 (Odell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on published biochemical studies.

claim: The TRPC4 structure misses 162 residues at the C-terminus.
source: Our structure of TRPC4 misses 162 residues at the C-terminus.
evidence: This is a description of what is not resolved in the structure.

claim: The missing C-terminal region comprises a PDZ-binding domain and a second IP3-binding domain and calmodulin binding sites.
source: This part of the protein comprises a PDZ-binding domain (Mery et al., 2002) and a second IP3-binding domain (Mery et al., 2001) and calmodulin binding sites (Tang et al., 2001; Trost et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on published biochemical characterization of these regions.

claim: The largest part of the missing C-terminal region is absent in the second most abundant splice variant of TRPC4, namely TRPC4β.
